mn2:0.2: The Discourse on All the Taints (Sabbāsava Sutta)
mn2:1.2: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn2:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn2:1.5: “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:2.1: “Monks, I shall teach you the way of restraining all the taints.
mn2:2.2: Listen and attend carefully, I will speak.”
mn2:2.3: “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:3.1: “Monks, I say that for one who knows and sees, the destruction of the taints occurs, not for one who does not know and does not see.
mn2:3.2: And what does he know, what does he see, whereby I say there is the destruction of the taints?
mn2:3.4: When one attends improperly, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase;
mn2:3.5: but when one attends properly, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:4.1: There are taints to be abandoned by seeing, taints to be abandoned by restraint, taints to be abandoned by using, taints to be abandoned by enduring, taints to be abandoned by avoiding, taints to be abandoned by removing, and taints to be abandoned by developing.
mn2:5.0: 1. Taints to be abandoned by seeing
mn2:5.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has no vision of the noble ones, is unskilled in the teaching of the noble ones, undisciplined in the teaching of the noble ones; who has no vision of good persons, unskilled in the teaching of good persons, undisciplined in the teaching of good persons—
mn2:5.3: does not understand what should be attended to, and does not understand what should not be attended to.
mn2:5.4: Not understanding what should be attended to and not understanding what should not be attended to, he attends to what should not be attended to, and he does not attend to what should be attended to.
mn2:6.1: And what, monks, are the things that should not be attended to, which he attends to?
mn2:6.2: When one attends to such things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases;
mn2:6.3: the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen taint of existence increases;
mn2:6.4: the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen taint of ignorance increases—
mn2:6.5: these are the things that should not be attended to, which he attends to.
mn2:6.6: And what, monks, are the things that should be attended to, which he does not attend to?
mn2:6.7: When one attends to such things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned;
mn2:6.8: the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned;
mn2:6.9: the unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:6.10: these are the things that should be attended to, which he does not attend to.
mn2:7.1: Because of his attending to what should not be attended to, and his not attending to what should be attended to, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase.
mn2:7.3: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past?’
mn2:7.4: ‘Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?’
mn2:7.5: Or else he is inwardly perplexed about the present thus:
mn2:7.6: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
mn2:8.1: For one who attends improperly in this way, one of six views arises:
mn2:8.2: The view ‘I have a self’ arises as true and established in him;
mn2:8.3: or the view ‘I have no self’ arises as true and established in him;
mn2:8.4: or the view ‘By means of self I perceive self’ arises as true and established in him;
mn2:8.5: or the view ‘By means of self I perceive not-self’ arises as true and established in him;
mn2:8.6: or the view ‘By means of not-self I perceive self’ arises as true and established in him;
mn2:8.7: or else he has this view:
mn2:8.8: ‘It is this self of mine that speaks and feels, and experiences here and there the result of good and bad actions; but this self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will endure as long as eternity.’
mn2:8.9: This, monks, is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a writhing of views, a fetter of views.
mn2:8.10: Bound by the fetter of views, monks, the uninstructed ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
mn2:8.11: I say he is not freed from suffering.
mn2:9.1: But, monks, an instructed noble disciple—
mn2:9.2: who has seen the noble ones, who is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, well trained in the teaching of the noble ones; who has seen good persons, skilled in the teaching of good persons, well trained in the teaching of good persons—
mn2:9.3: understands what should be attended to and what should not be attended to.
mn2:9.4: Understanding what should be attended to and what should not be attended to, he does not attend to what should not be attended to, and he attends to what should be attended to.
mn2:10.1: And what, monks, are the things that should not be attended to, which he does not attend to?
mn2:10.2: When one attends to such things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases;
mn2:10.3: the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen taint of existence increases;
mn2:10.4: the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen taint of ignorance increases—
mn2:10.5: these are the things that should not be attended to, which he does not attend to.
mn2:10.6: And what, monks, are the things that should be attended to, which he attends to?
mn2:10.7: When one attends to such things, the unarisen taint of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen taint of sensual desire is abandoned;
mn2:10.8: the unarisen taint of existence does not arise, and the arisen taint of existence is abandoned;
mn2:10.9: the unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:10.10: these are the things that should be attended to, which he attends to.
mn2:10.11: Because of his not attending to what should not be attended to, and his attending to what should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:11.1: He attends properly: ‘This is suffering’; he attends properly: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he attends properly: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he attends properly: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
mn2:11.2: For him who attends properly in this way, three fetters are abandoned:
mn2:11.3: identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of rules and vows.
mn2:11.4: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing.
mn2:12.0: 2. Taints to be abandoned by restraint
mn2:12.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint?
mn2:12.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, lives restrained in the restraint of eye-sense;
mn2:12:3: If one lives without restraining the restraint of eye-sense, taints would arise as afflictions; if with restraint, those same taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:12.4: He lives restrained, with reflection, in the restraint of ear-sense …
mn2:12.9: If one lives without restraining the restraint of mind-sense, taints would arise; if with restraint, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:12.10: If one lives without restraint generally, taints would arise; with restraint, they would not be afflictions.
mn2:12.11: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by restraint.
mn2:13.0: 3. Taints to be abandoned by proper use
mn2:13.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by proper use?
mn2:13.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, properly uses his robe:
mn2:13.3: ‘Only to oppose cold, heat, insects, dust, dew; for modesty; for the maintenance of the body; for non-harm; for supporting the holy life.’
mn2:14.2: ‘Not for two meals, not for indulgence, not for ornamentation, not for beautification; only for sustaining the body, for health, for supporting the holy life; I reject past pain, will not generate new pain; my motion shall be harmless, modest, upright.’
mn2:15.1: He properly uses his dwelling, thinking:
mn2:15.2: ‘Only to oppose cold, heat, insects, wind, for suitable seclusion.’
mn2:16.1: He properly uses medicines and requisites for the sick, thinking:
mn2:16.2: ‘Only to oppose arising painful feelings, for alleviation of suffering.’
mn2:17.1: If one lives without proper use, taints would arise as afflictions; with proper use, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:17.2: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by proper use.
mn2:18.0: 4. Taints to be abandoned by endurance
mn2:18.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by endurance?
mn2:18.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, endures cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the contact of gad-flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, snakes;
mn2:18.3: If one lived without endurance, taints would arise; with endurance, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:18.4: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by endurance.
mn2:19.0: 5. Taints to be abandoned by avoidance
mn2:19.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by avoidance?
mn2:19.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, avoids a violent elephant, a violent ass, a violent ox, a violent dog, a snake, a knife, a thorny place, a precipitous cliff, a dangerous tree.
mn2:19.3: In suitable fashion he sits off the path, moves off the road, does not associate with bad companions; wise recluse will avoid evil places and evil association, doing this by avoidance.
mn2:19.4: If one lives without avoidance, taints would arise; with avoidance, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:19.5: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by avoidance.
mn2:20.0: 6. Taints to be abandoned by removal
mn2:20.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by removal?
mn2:20.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, when a sensual thought arises, does not bear it, he casts it aside, removes it, destroys it, makes it not be; likewise for hostile and unwholesome thoughts.
mn2:20.3: If one lives without removal, taints would arise; with removal, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:20.4: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by removal.
mn2:21.0: 7. Taints to be abandoned by cultivation
mn2:21.1: And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by cultivation?
mn2:21.2: Here, monks, a monk, with reflection, cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, dependent on seclusion, free from desire and discontent, leading to relinquishment;
mn2:21.3: He cultivates the factor of investigation of dhammas …
mn2:21.8: … the factor of equanimity, dependent on seclusion, free from desire and discontent, leading to relinquishment.
mn2:21.9: If one lives without cultivation, taints would arise; with cultivation, those taints would not be afflictions.
mn2:21.10: These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by cultivation.
mn2:22.1: Because, monks, for the monk whose taints to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned by seeing, whose taints to be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned by restraint, whose taints to be abandoned by use have been abandoned by use, whose taints to be abandoned by endurance have been abandoned by endurance, whose taints to be abandoned by avoidance have been abandoned by avoidance, whose taints to be abandoned by removal have been abandoned by removal, whose taints to be abandoned by cultivation have been abandoned by cultivation,
mn2:22.2: that monk is called one who dwells restrained with regard to all taints; he has cut off craving, broken the fetters, and, by right insight into conceit, made an end to suffering and stress.
mn2:22.3: That is what the Blessed One said.
mn2:22.4: Delighted, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
mn2:22.5: Thus ends the Sabbāsava Sutta, the second.
